claims.text: The starting material is a uniform, fine-lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy's strength and plasticity are below industrial application requirements.
Adding approximately 0.5 at% Hf will produce Hf-rich precipitates at or within the lamellar interfaces.
Hf-rich precipitates impede grain-boundary sliding.
Hf-rich precipitates impede dislocation movement.
The Hf-induced precipitates will stabilize the lamellar interfaces.
Interface stabilization by Hf may maintain a more uniform and robust passive film.
The Hf addition will increase yield strength and tensile strength relative to the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
The Hf addition will increase ductility relative to the unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
The Hf addition will improve room-temperature creep resistance.
The Hf addition will improve corrosion resistance in chloride-containing sulfuric acid.
The Hf-modified alloy will perform better during extreme temperature fluctuations and long-term mechanical loading.
In unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1, the passive film is stable at low temperature but unstable at high temperature in chloride-containing sulfuric acid.
Unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 undergoes B2-phase pitting at 5 °C and pitting plus dissolution at room temperature and above in chloride-containing sulfuric acid.
Lamellar-interface weaknesses in the unmodified alloy contribute to cracking under mechanical and corrosive stresses.
Hf additions have improved high-temperature strength and ductility in a similar dual-phase high-entropy alloy.
The optimum Hf concentration may require tuning because mechanical performance varies non-monotonically with Hf content.
The improvements are expected to apply within service ranges typical of fasteners but may be limited outside tested temperature and corrosion ranges.
A controlled comparison of 0.5 at% Hf-modified and unmodified samples under thermal cycling, room-temperature creep, tensile, corrosion, and microscopy tests can evaluate the hypothesis.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified alloy fails to show statistically significant improvements in all listed mechanical, creep, and corrosion outcomes relative to the control.
